newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Germany under pressure to back EU film fund.
newsitem.headline: Germany under pressure to back EU film fund.

text.p: Germany will come under pressure on Monday to lift opposition to a guarantee fund for the European Union's audiovisual industry which the sector says could help create two million jobs over the next 10 years.

Diplomats say Germany's position is pivotal to the outcome of an EU culture ministers' meeting in Luxembourg, although the Netherlands, Sweden and Britain also harbour reservations about the plan for a five-year 60-million-Ecu ($67 million) fund.
"Really the issue is the German position," the chairman of the European Parliament's culture committee, Peter Pex, told reporters.

Although there is no prospect of the ministers reaching agreement on Monday, they will seek to open the way to a decision during Luxembourg's six-month presidency of the bloc, which starts on Tuesday.
Pex said German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had responded well to a plea from French President Jacques Chirac to back the plan, but that the blockage lay with Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
"The Germans are blocked by the idea that they should not spend a penny more on European affairs," he said.

Facing a $6 billion trade deficit with the United States, the European film sector says it needs the financial incentive to take risks, and that the EU money could trigger 300 million Ecus ($340 million) in investment.

"Is Europe serious about taking a share of the audiovisual growth or are we going to leave it to outsiders to benefit from this growth market?" Philippe Kern, spokesman for the European Film Companies Alliance, which groups the major industry players, told reporters.

The ministers will be meeting against a backdrop of mounting frustration at Germany's inability on constitutional grounds to endorse EU cultural policy decisions, which need to be adopted unanimously.
Germany's regional states are responsible for cultural matters and have reacted negatively to previous moves by the federal government in Bonn to endorse EU cultural legislation.

Fearing a legal challenge by the states, Germany blocked a move to install qualified majority voting on cultural matters in the closing stages of the EU treaty review in Amsterdam on June 16-17, meaning the same blockage could arise over the next few years.
The EU Commissioner for Culture, Marcelino Oreja, told Reuters he felt "a certain frustration" at the situation and predicted paralysis in the the EU's cultural policy.
He said he would ask the German states whether they wanted to be responsible for blocking EU cultural policy, and ask them to find a way of cooperating.

Germany recently infuriated the European Parliament by single-handedly blocking a compromise on a fund, dubbed Raphael, to help preserve the EU's cultural heritage, from museums to libraries and archeological sites. ($ = 0.886 European Currency Unit ECUs)
